power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: The way in which induction is applied shapes the field of consciousness science, as scientists draw inferences about experience, generalise neural signatures, and make projections across different contexts.
Although deduction establishes ideals of certainty, induction directs experimentation and decision-making.

The present article gives a comprehensive examination of the role of induction in consciousness science by looking at its philosophical roots, from Aristotle and Hume through to Popper, Salmon, and Peirce, and by considering its formal expression in Bayesian and predictive-processing frameworks.

It then looks at how induction functions in the areas of neuroimaging, comparative cognition, and clinical practice, pointing out the achievements (such as pattern detection, the monitoring of anaesthesia, and the detection of covert awareness) as well as the structural dangers (including the slip between correlation and causation, overgeneralisation, anthropomorphism, and misclassification at high stakes).

Recent syntheses that are oriented towards sufficiency (for example, Coppola, 2025;Mashour et al., 2020; Hohwy et al., 2020) show both the strength and the dangers of inductive generalisation by extending correlational results into assertions of ontological sufficiency.
text.formatted: Recent syntheses that are oriented towards sufficiency (for example, Coppola, 2025;<ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Mashour et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Hohwy et al., 2020)</ref> show both the strength and the dangers of inductive generalisation by extending correlational results into assertions of ontological sufficiency.

text.text: Drawing on the latest criticisms and on adversarial comparisons of the major theories, the article advocates for an explicitly deflationary approach which maintains that induction is essential but must be kept within limits.

The key tools involved are: (i) operational vocabularies that distinguish between constructs (such as access, arousal, valuation, and metacognition); (ii) clear bridge principles that connect observables to experiences; and (iii) prediction tables that record both positive predictions and potential falsifiers.
This practical framework does not resolve Hume's problem; rather, it makes our inductive commitments manageable, testable, and ethically responsible.
The study of consciousness should continue to be inductive, but it should not be inflationary.

To show the feasibility of this system, the paper includes examples of bridge principles and quantitative criteria for "bounded" inference, such as Bayesian probabilities, model-comparison metrics, and causal diagrams.
The ethical and institutional aspects are also broadened to cover AI, animal, and algorithmic induction.
These additions connect philosophical modesty with the practical implementation of methodology and with moral accountability.

Scientific discourse tends to give more weight to deduction, but in reality research is mostly inductive, involving the formulation of generalizations based on empirical cases and the application of observed regularities to new situations (Popper, 2005; Salmon, 2017).

text.text: In the case of consciousness research, this inductive approach is particularly clear: scientists deduce subjective experience from behavioral and neural data, generalize correlations across different paradigms, and extend their findings from one species to another or between different clinical states (Crick & Koch, 1990; Koch et al., 2016).

text.text: A similar sufficiencyoriented approach is also found in major theoretical models.

The Global Neuronal Workspace models (Mashour et al., 2020) and the predictive-processing accounts (Hohwy & Seth, 2020) both describe consciousness in terms of hierarchical integration of evidence, whether this is described as cortical "ignition" or as precision-weighted inference.

text.text: Each of these frameworks captures important regularities in both clinical and experimental situations, but both are at risk of overreaching when they treat functional or statistical coherence as if it were causal closure.

In this context, such models require bounded induction: their explanatory power depends on transparent bridge principles linking brain activity to conscious access and on formally identifying falsifiers through model comparison and counterfactual testing.

text.text: With these tools it is possible to carry out simulations and compare quantitative models, turning conceptual differences into analyses that can be tested empirically.

The idea of sufficiency also needs to be made clearer: empirical sufficiency means statistical adequacy in terms of prediction, while ontological sufficiency implies a metaphysical adequacy for experience (Achinstein, 2001; Feest, 2022a; 2022b).

text.text: The first of these supports valid inductive generalisation; the second is a modal overextension.
By keeping this distinction, a deflationary inductive programme can be maintained which is empirically rigorous yet philosophically cautious.

In theoretical models of consciousness, induction is not limited to empirical data but also involves evolutionary reasoning that connects neural organisation to supposed forms of experience (Birch et al., 2020; Godfrey-Smith, 2016).

text.text: Approaches that aim to establish affective consciousness in vertebrates generally base their conclusions on the shared subcortical architectures and behavioural repertoires found in different species (Feinberg & Mallatt, 2017).
text.formatted: Approaches that aim to establish affective consciousness in vertebrates generally base their conclusions on the shared subcortical architectures and behavioural repertoires found in different species <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Feinberg & Mallatt, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: These theories suggest that the conserved neural circuits which play a role in affective regulation might be the basis for similar experiential abilities among various animals, for example pain-like states in fish.

Yet the leap from homology to phenomenology is still inductive and not deductive: it assumes that functional or structural continuity means there is also continuity of experience, a assumption which must be carefully examined in order to prevent anthropomorphic projection (Birch et al., 2020; Feest, 2022a; 2022b).

text.text: Within a deflationary inductive framework, it would be necessary to have explicit bridge principles that specify how neural homology could correspond to phenomenological analogy and also identify possible empirical falsifiers of that correspondence (Koch et al., 2016; Feest, 2022a; 2022b).

In the same way that evolutionary programs arrive at the concept of consciousness by drawing inferences from neural homology, phenomenology-first approaches do so by referencing experiential examples.
These programs frequently assert that they are able to deduce universal structures from lived experience.

However, in reality they depend on inductively gathering phenomenological cases from pathology, psychiatry, and perception in order to support their claims regarding minimal selfhood and temporal experience (Zahavi, 2025).

text.text: In recent years, research in the philosophy of mind and neuroscience has aimed at bringing firstperson phenomenological accounts in line with neural data, with the goal of connecting subjective experience to physiological explanations (Feest, 2022a; 2022b; Martínez, 2025).

text.text: Although these 'neurophenomenological' approaches strive for integration, they are still based on inductive reasoning: in order to make generalisations from individual cases, it is necessary to have explicit bridge principles that specify how experiential categories such as agency, affect, or the feeling of temporal flow relate to neural measures (Craver, 2007).

text.text: If those mappings are not established, these programmes could end up replacing metaphysical overreaching with methodological indeterminacy, thus highlighting the importance of adopting a deflationary approach when extending phenomenological inference into empirical settings (Feest, 2022a; 2022b; Koch et al., 2016).

In the field of theoretical models, the search for the Neural Correlates of Consciousness (NCCs) shows both the strengths and weaknesses of inductive reasoning in the study of consciousness (Koch et al., 2016; Seth & Bayne, 2022).

text.text: Since Crick and Koch's initial suggestion in 1990, the NCC project has advanced by inferring neural substrates of awareness from observed correlations.

Various competing theories highlight different statistical patterns: posterior cortical activity for phenomenal content (Boly et al., 2017), prefrontal activation for global access (Baars, Geld, & Kozma, 2021; Dehaene & Changeux, 2011), recurrent interactions for temporal synthesis, and informational complexity for intrinsic structural unity (Tononi, 2004).

text.text: As these features often occur together, the same data sets can lead to several incompatible inductive generalisations.

None of the current NCC frameworks can assert that a particular feature is necessary or sufficient without having undergone counterfactual validation or having carried out explicit causal tests (Feest, 2022a; 2022b; Koch et al., 2016).

text.text: In order to reduce inductive inflation, formal prediction tables and falsifiability matrices are needed in order to clearly differentiate between positive predictions and disconfirming results (Michel & Morales, 2020; Seth & Bayne, 2022).

text.text: These tools transform the NCC endeavour from one of simply accumulating correlations to one based on a deflationary and testable logic of inference.
Although there are legitimate reasons to be cautious about the use of induction, there is no doubt about its necessity for the study of consciousness.
Since subjective experience cannot be directly measured, it has to be inferred from behavioural, physiological, and neural regularities (Koch et al., 2016; Seth & Bayne, 2022).
text.formatted: Since subjective experience cannot be directly measured, it has to be inferred from behavioural, physiological, and neural regularities <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Koch et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Seth & Bayne, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Induction therefore provides a link between observable patterns and the unobservable phenomenon of subjective experience, allowing empirical access to subjective phenomena by means of systematic inference (Feest, 2022a; 2022b).
text.formatted: Induction therefore provides a link between observable patterns and the unobservable phenomenon of subjective experience, allowing empirical access to subjective phenomena by means of systematic inference <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Feest, 2022a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">2022b)</ref>.

text.text: The practical advantages of induction are evident in a variety of methodological situations: for example, in detecting patterns in complex or noisy data (Koch et al., 2016), in guiding prediction and control in clinical situations such as those involving EEG trajectories during anaesthesia (Purdon et al., 2013), in making cross-species and developmental inferences wherein verbal reports are not available (Emery & Clayton, 2004; Feinberg & Mallatt, 2017), and in helping to make prognostic and diagnostic judgments in disorders of consciousness (Owen et al., 2006; Schnakers et al., 2009).

text.text: Induction thus continues to function as a practical tool for the purpose of finding and prediction.

Its worth is not in proving metaphysical necessity yet in securing empirical adequacy-this being precisely the methodological humility at the heart of a deflationary inductive approach (Feest, 2022a; 2022b; Koch et al., 2016).

The deflationary inductive programme can be put into practice using explicit and testable tools such as prediction tables and bridge matrices which link observed neural and behavioural variables to phenomenological constructs while assigning evidential weights (Feest, 2022a; 2022b; Craver, 2007).

text.text: Comparable inferential difficulties also arise in major theoretical approaches.

In the Global Neuronal Workspace theory (Mashour et al., 2020), cortical 'ignition' is often presented as a sign of conscious access, while predictive-processing accounts (Hohwy & Seth, 2020) see hierarchical precision-weighting as a means of carrying out phenomenological updating.

text.text: Although both models present plausible causal structures, each can shift from being based on evidence to asserting ontological sufficiency when their formal coherence is regarded as proof of necessity.

Within a deflationary inductive framework, such theoretical inferences must remain explicitly provisional-limited by bridge principles that specify how neural integration or predictive optimisation translate into attributions of experience, and open to being refuted by adversarial model testing.

There is a danger in this line of reasoning in that it could replace explanatory adequacy with predictive accuracy -just as happens in the case of overfitting, where generalization goes beyond what the evidence allows (Etz & Vandekerckhove, 2018; Penny et al., 2010).

text.text: Moreover, by systematically publishing prediction tables which include counterfactual falsifiers (for example, lesion, stimulation, or pharmacological dissociation studies) the inductive reasoning remains firmly grounded in empirical evidence and is also methodologically capable of self-correction (Koch et al., 2016; Feest, 2022a; 2022b).

text.text: On the other hand, cortical lesion data indicating reduced responsiveness are sufficient to support claims of functional necessity, not of phenomenal exclusivity (Boly et al., 2017; Giacino & Smart, 2007).

text.text: Both approaches risk overreaching their inductive justification by failing to account for the bridging assumptions that connect brain activity to experiential attribution (Craver, 2007; Woodward, 2005; Feest, 2022a; 2022b).

text.text: A deflationary inductive framework reduces this risk by asking researchers, in every inference, to specify three parameters of generalization:  What is the scope?
That is, which organisms, states, and modalities are covered?
 What is the causal or functional structure that underlies the generalization?
 What empirical results would lead to its retraction?
By including these parameters in the prediction tables (Penny et al., 2010), inductive reasoning would remain empirically rigorous while preventing it from being inflated into metaphysical necessity.

text.text: In the field of comparative cognition, inductive projection typically takes the form of anthropomorphism, which involves inferring human-like consciousness from the flexible or intelligent behaviour of non-human species (Birch et al., 2020; Godfrey-Smith, 2016).

Cases like corvids solving problems, dolphins showing self-recognition, and cephalopods engaging in social planning lead people to draw comparisons with human mental abilities (Emery & Clayton, 2004; Godfrey-Smith, 2016).
text.formatted: Cases like corvids solving problems, dolphins showing self-recognition, and cephalopods engaging in social planning lead people to draw comparisons with human mental abilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Emery & Clayton, 2004</ref>; Godfrey-Smith, 2016).

text.text: Although these behaviours indicate a high level of cognition, they do not on their own imply any phenomenological similarity.

The leap from functional similarity to experiential resemblance relies on unexamined bridge principles that claim mechanistic homology or behavioural convergence implies experiential homology-a kind of conceptual shift that has not been supported by empirical evidence (Birch et al., 2020; Feest, 2022a; 2022b).

The evolutionary model proposed by Feinberg and Mallatt (2017) shows this double-edged reasoning: their careful inference based on conserved subcortical architectures allows for a reasonable generalisation regarding affective consciousness among vertebrates, but when applied to shared phenomenality it may go beyond what the evidence justifies.

text.text: This excessive reach is similar to the claims about cortical or subcortical sufficiency in human neuroscience (Koch et al., 2016; Feest, 2022a; 2022b), showing a common tendency to move from empirical regularities to ontological conclusions.

text.text: In order to prevent this kind of drift, a deflationary inductive framework demands that three parameters be explicitly stated when making inferences across species:  What aspect of consciousness is in question here (for example, affect, perception, or metacognition)?
 What empirical relationship justifies mapping functional analogies onto phenomenological claims?
 What counterexamples-for instance, those showing a discrepancy between neural homology and behavioral flexibility-could be used to refute that inference?

By including these criteria in the prediction tables (Penny et al., 2010; Feest, 2022a; 2022b) the heuristic value of the comparative data is maintained while avoiding the situation in which similarity turns into assumed sameness.
It is true that consciousness might be multi-realizable, but its recognition has to be carried out with methodological restraint rather than through empathetic projection.
In the field of clinical neuroscience, the most serious inductive mistakes occur when clinicians incorrectly classify consciousness on the basis of behaviour.
For many years, the lack of a motor report was considered to be enough proof of unconsciousness -a practical yet fragile inductive rule (Laureys et al., 2004; Koch et al., 2016).

text.text: This belief was challenged when studies using neuroimaging and EEG techniques showed that patients who had been diagnosed as being in a vegetative state could in fact carry out covert commands (Owen et al., 2006; Schnakers et al., 2009).

A deflationary inductive framework would overcome this by requiring explicit scope conditions (i.e. specifying which patients, states, and modalities the inference applies to) and counterfactual disconfirmers (for example, covert imagery tasks or evoked potential tests) for each diagnostic inference (Koch et al., 2016; Penny et al., 2010).

text.text: Including these in standardised prediction tables would make clinical inference more transparent and replicable while helping to prevent misclassification of patients in a categorical way.

The ethical consequences are important: in cases involving disorders of consciousness, inductive errors have both moral and epistemic implications, influencing decisions about treatment, rehabilitation and life support (Yuste et al., 2017).

text.text: Inductive discipline therefore takes on the role of a form of clinical care -ensuring that epistemic humility informs practice in situations where error is existential (Feest, 2022a; 2022b).
A further structural risk is the increasing use of algorithmic induction in both neuroscience and clinical diagnosis.

Nowadays, machine-learning models are able to identify putative "neural signatures of consciousness" and to classify different brain states from high-dimensional EEG or fMRI data-yet frequently lack any clear causal or conceptual basis (Burrell, 2016; Creel, 2020; Samek et al., 2017).

text.text: Such systems show what Burrell (2016) refers to as epistemic opacity: the pathways by which they make their inferences may be impossible for even the developers to understand, which in turn makes it hard to validate or falsify them.
Algorithmic induction therefore inherits and, in many cases, worsens the same weaknesses as human inductive reasoning (Feest, 2022a; 2022b).

text.text: These epistemic failures have ethical implications: the opacity of algorithms used in anaesthesia monitoring or in the diagnosis of disorders of consciousness can result in misclassifications with serious moral and clinical consequences (Yuste et al., 2017; Topol, 2019).

text.text: Therefore, a deflationary inductive framework must also apply to machine inference, requiring interpretable architectures, explicit statements of prior assumptions, and auditable prediction tables that make algorithms' inductive claims empirically testable and falsifiable (Samek et al., 2017; Feest, 2022a; 2022b).

text.text: The moral significance of induction in the study of consciousness goes beyond mere attention to epistemic rigor; for when inductive inferences are not carefully examined, they lead to errors which have effects on humans, animals, and society.

It is for this reason that a disciplined approach to induction is both a methodological and a moral requirement-because it determines how recognition, rights, and care are allocated in situations of uncertainty (Feest, 2022a; 2022b; Yuste et al., 2017).
text.formatted: It is for this reason that a disciplined approach to induction is both a methodological and a moral requirement-because it determines how recognition, rights, and care are allocated in situations of uncertainty <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Feest, 2022a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">2022b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Yuste et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text:  Clinical ethics: in cases of disorders of consciousness, making an inductive misclassification has a direct impact on questions of life, death, and dignity.

The longstanding assumption that the lack of motor response means there is no consciousnessalthough once a helpful rule of thumb-has now been refuted by empirical research (Owen et al., 2006; Schnakers et al., 2009).
text.formatted: The longstanding assumption that the lack of motor response means there is no consciousnessalthough once a helpful rule of thumb-has now been refuted by empirical research <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Owen et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Schnakers et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, the moral consequences of this assumption remain, affecting choices regarding care, rehabilitation, and the status of a person as a person (Laureys et al., 2004; Giacino & Smart, 2007).
text.formatted: Nevertheless, the moral consequences of this assumption remain, affecting choices regarding care, rehabilitation, and the status of a person as a person <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Laureys et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Giacino & Smart, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: In this context, inductive humility should be regarded as an ethical principle: doctors must treat any diagnostic inference as temporary, open to being proven wrong, and willing to adjust it in the light of counterevidence (Yuste et al., 2017; Feest, 2022a; 2022b).
text.formatted: In this context, inductive humility should be regarded as an ethical principle: doctors must treat any diagnostic inference as temporary, open to being proven wrong, and willing to adjust it in the light of counterevidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Yuste et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Feest, 2022a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">2022b)</ref>.

text.text:  Ethics from a comparative and regulatory point of view: inflationary inductive arguments about animal or subcortical consciousness have important consequences for welfare policy.

Examples of programmes which conclude that affective consciousness exists on the basis of neural homology or behavioural flexibility (Feinberg & Mallatt, 2017; Birch et al., 2020; Godfrey-Smith, 2016) show the conflict between moral caution and evidential rigor.

text.text: It is possible to give ethical protections a prudent justification-on the grounds of uncertainty and the possibility of harm-without having to assume that there is phenomenological sameness.
Hence, inductive discipline promotes both compassion and epistemic caution (Feest, 2022a; 2022b).
text.formatted: Hence, inductive discipline promotes both compassion and epistemic caution <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Feest, 2022a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">2022b)</ref>.

text.text:  The idea of artificial intelligence and neuro-rights is that anthropomorphic projection reappears in new forms in AI and neurotechnology.
Adaptive or conversational machinelearning systems are frequently described in mentalistic language-that is, by going from pattern recognition to claiming sentience (Metzinger, 2021; Gabriel, 2020).
text.formatted: Adaptive or conversational machinelearning systems are frequently described in mentalistic language-that is, by going from pattern recognition to claiming sentience <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Metzinger, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Gabriel, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: When it comes to ethical responsibility, there must be care regarding ontology: it is necessary to differentiate between computational inference and subjective self-modeling.
A similar caution is needed in the case of brain-computer interfaces, since drawing too hasty a conclusion from neural decoding to personhood could lead to distortion of policy.
Frameworks for neuro-rights (Yuste et al., 2017) exemplify bounded induction: they aim to safeguard mental privacy and autonomy without confusing a neural signal with experience itself.
text.formatted: Frameworks for neuro-rights <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Yuste et al., 2017)</ref> exemplify bounded induction: they aim to safeguard mental privacy and autonomy without confusing a neural signal with experience itself.

text.text: In all clinical, comparative, and artificial situations, a deflationary inductive framework thus serves as a moral and methodological guide.

It achieves this by incorporating clear bridge principles, transparent prediction tables, and falsifiable hypotheses into the chains of inference, thereby establishing epistemic humility in which inferential errors have ethical implications (Feest, 2022a; 2022b; Penny et al., 2010).
text.formatted: It achieves this by incorporating clear bridge principles, transparent prediction tables, and falsifiable hypotheses into the chains of inference, thereby establishing epistemic humility in which inferential errors have ethical implications <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Feest, 2022a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">2022b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Penny et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Induction must therefore be both empirically limited and morally reflective: a science of consciousness that bases its integrity on its own recognition of limitations (Feest, 2022a; 2022b; Koch et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Induction must therefore be both empirically limited and morally reflective: a science of consciousness that bases its integrity on its own recognition of limitations <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Feest, 2022a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">2022b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Koch et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Induction in science is never entirely a matter of individuals alone; it is organised in a social way and supported by institutions (Feest, 2022a; 2022b; Chambers, 2019).
text.formatted: Induction in science is never entirely a matter of individuals alone; it is organised in a social way and supported by institutions <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Feest, 2022a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">2022b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Chambers, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The reward systems which determine scientific value, the incentives encouraging novelty, the citation hierarchies, and the practice of selective publication all tend to favour bold generalisations over careful inference (Fanelli, 2010).
text.formatted: The reward systems which determine scientific value, the incentives encouraging novelty, the citation hierarchies, and the practice of selective publication all tend to favour bold generalisations over careful inference <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Fanelli, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Correlations which might still be regarded as tentative if epistemic humility were taken into account are often inflated into assertions of necessity because of the pressures related to attention and prestige that characterise the publication culture.
The kind of inferential overreach that is apparent is therefore usually just an institutional feature (Feest, 2022a; 2022b).
text.formatted: The kind of inferential overreach that is apparent is therefore usually just an institutional feature <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Feest, 2022a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">2022b)</ref>.

text.text: The replication problems in psychology and neuroscience (Nosek et al., 2015) show that the weakness of inductive generalization usually stems from social factors rather than merely from methodological defects.
text.formatted: The replication problems in psychology and neuroscience <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Nosek et al., 2015)</ref> show that the weakness of inductive generalization usually stems from social factors rather than merely from methodological defects.

text.text: If replication, falsification, and transparency are given less importance than innovation and narrative coherence, inductive conclusions tend to become accepted without being examined (Chambers, 2019; Feest, 2022a; 2022b).

The issue is not generalization per se but the social imbalance between the incentives for making discoveries and those for correcting them; an imbalance which encourages overreaching while failing to provide sufficient funding for self-criticism (Fanelli, 2010).
text.formatted: The issue is not generalization per se but the social imbalance between the incentives for making discoveries and those for correcting them; an imbalance which encourages overreaching while failing to provide sufficient funding for self-criticism <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Fanelli, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: A pragmatic inductivism that is to be sustainable therefore has to serve as both an epistemic virtue and an institutional design principle.
Procedures such as pre-registration, open data requirements, and adversarial collaboration (Chambers, 2019; Nosek et al., 2015) turn humility into a feature of collective practice.
text.formatted: Procedures such as pre-registration, open data requirements, and adversarial collaboration <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Chambers, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Nosek et al., 2015)</ref> turn humility into a feature of collective practice.

text.text: Meta-scientific innovations, registered replication reports and Bayesian meta-analysis (Etz & Vandekerckhove, 2018) extend the deflationary attitude of bounded induction from individual reasoning to the regulation of scientific practice (Feest, 2022a; 2022b).
text.formatted: Meta-scientific innovations, registered replication reports and Bayesian meta-analysis (Etz & Vandekerckhove, 2018) extend the deflationary attitude of bounded induction from individual reasoning to the regulation of scientific practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Feest, 2022a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">2022b)</ref>.

text.text: In this respect, bounded induction functions as a social technology; it is a decentralized system of epistemic safeguards which prevents overgeneralization, reduces confirmation cascades, and brings modesty in line with integrity.
The logic of induction, after having been incorporated into methodological frameworks, has now to be established within the natural environment of science.

The Bayesian and predictive-processing approaches treat induction as probabilistic updating, a dynamic process in which hypotheses are improved by reducing prediction error (Clark, 2015; Hohwy, 2013).
text.formatted: The Bayesian and predictive-processing approaches treat induction as probabilistic updating, a dynamic process in which hypotheses are improved by reducing prediction error <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Clark, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Hohwy, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Perception, action, and learning are all brought together within a hierarchical system of belief revision: the brain functions as a kind of prediction machine that works out the causes of its sensory inputs.

The Free Energy Principle (Friston, 2010) takes this line of reasoning and turns it into a general theory of adaptive systems, stating that all self-organizing agents act in order to minimize surprise.
text.formatted: The Free Energy Principle <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Friston, 2010)</ref> takes this line of reasoning and turns it into a general theory of adaptive systems, stating that all self-organizing agents act in order to minimize surprise.

text.text: However, although this broad scope is attractive in its simplicity, it calls for epistemic caution since it may obscure the inductive assumptions that are built into its own formalism (Gershman, 2019; Feest, 2022a; 2022b).
text.formatted: However, although this broad scope is attractive in its simplicity, it calls for epistemic caution since it may obscure the inductive assumptions that are built into its own formalism <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Gershman, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Feest, 2022a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">2022b)</ref>.

text.text: Bayesian inference might seem to bring induction under control: priors limit the extent of generalization, posteriors measure belief revision, and precision-weighting adjusts the level of confidence (Etz & Vandekerckhove, 2018).
text.formatted: Bayesian inference might seem to bring induction under control: priors limit the extent of generalization, posteriors measure belief revision, and precision-weighting adjusts the level of confidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Etz & Vandekerckhove, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, as Parvizi-Wayne (2025) points out, mathematical tractability does not mean that a theory is explanatorily adequate.

In the field of consciousness research, predictive and free-energy frameworks have a tendency to treat inductive assumptions as if they were actual empirical discoveries, confusing a high degree of model fit with real causal or phenomenological insight (Koch et al., 2016; Feest, 2022a Feest, , 2022b)).
text.formatted: In the field of consciousness research, predictive and free-energy frameworks have a tendency to treat inductive assumptions as if they were actual empirical discoveries, confusing a high degree of model fit with real causal or phenomenological insight <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Koch et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Feest, 2022a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Feest, , 2022b))</ref>.

text.text: The recent reinterpretation of predictive processing as a model of adaptive control rather than as a complete explanation (Poth et al., 2025) is an example of a careful and deflationary stance: by focusing on embodiment, ecological constraints, and bounded rationality, it maintains formal induction within the bounds of empirical and conceptual limitations.

text.text: A similar development occurs in the area of causal discovery.
Directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and causal Bayesian networks (Pearl, 2009) express inductive structure by connecting statistical dependencies to possible interventions.
text.formatted: Directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and causal Bayesian networks <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Pearl, 2009)</ref> express inductive structure by connecting statistical dependencies to possible interventions.

text.text: When bridge principles are included as constraints in such graphs, inductive relationships become falsifiable; that is, correlations can be tested against counterfactual simulations or causal experiments (Woodward, 2005; Penny et al., 2010).
text.formatted: When bridge principles are included as constraints in such graphs, inductive relationships become falsifiable; that is, correlations can be tested against counterfactual simulations or causal experiments <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Woodward, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Penny et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The combination of probabilistic and causal modelling reflects the practical spirit of bounded induction: it involves explicit priors, clear bridges, and testable falsifiers (Feest, 2022a; 2022b).
text.formatted: The combination of probabilistic and causal modelling reflects the practical spirit of bounded induction: it involves explicit priors, clear bridges, and testable falsifiers <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Feest, 2022a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">2022b)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, Bayesian frameworks do not resolve Hume's problem of induction-they instead operationalize it.

Their philosophical strength does not lie in logical certainty but in computational accountability: they make inductive commitments explicit, quantifiable, and open to correction (Carnap, 1950; Keynes, 2013; Etz & Vandekerckhove, 2018).
text.formatted: Their philosophical strength does not lie in logical certainty but in computational accountability: they make inductive commitments explicit, quantifiable, and open to correction <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Carnap, 1950;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Keynes, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Etz & Vandekerckhove, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In consciousness science, where inferences can affect theoretical validity and moral responsibility, this formalization acts as a form of ethical discipline (Feest, 2022a; 2022b; Yuste et al., 2017).
text.formatted: In consciousness science, where inferences can affect theoretical validity and moral responsibility, this formalization acts as a form of ethical discipline <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Feest, 2022a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">2022b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Yuste et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The most sharp criticisms of contemporary consciousness science all lead to the same conclusion: there is inductive inflation caused by a lack of empirical and conceptual constraints (Block, 2019; Seth & Bayne, 2022; Feest, 2022a; 2022b). Block (2019) cautions that neural markers which are correlational in nature, for example P3b activity or posterior "hot-zone" activations, are too easily treated as necessary or sufficient conditions for consciousness, particularly in "no-report" paradigms in which behavioural verification is separated from subjective inference (Duman et al., 2022).
text.formatted: The most sharp criticisms of contemporary consciousness science all lead to the same conclusion: there is inductive inflation caused by a lack of empirical and conceptual constraints <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Block, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Seth & Bayne, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Feest, 2022a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">2022b)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Block (2019)</ref> cautions that neural markers which are correlational in nature, for example P3b activity or posterior "hot-zone" activations, are too easily treated as necessary or sufficient conditions for consciousness, particularly in "no-report" paradigms in which behavioural verification is separated from subjective inference <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Duman et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Seth and Bayne (2022) go on to develop this criticism by pointing out that major theories, such as the global workspace, recurrent processing, and integrated information, tend to gather data that is compatible with them without making any predictions that can be used to discriminate between the models or that are capable of being falsified.

The resulting diversity of views does not stem from an abundance of evidence but rather from a lack of constraint: different models are able to fit the same data because their inductive commitments are not clearly defined (Michel & Morales, 2020).
text.formatted: The resulting diversity of views does not stem from an abundance of evidence but rather from a lack of constraint: different models are able to fit the same data because their inductive commitments are not clearly defined <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Michel & Morales, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Philosophers who have considered scientific explanation have for a long time warned against such uncontrolled generalisation.

Mechanistic approaches call for the explicit identification of the components and the way in which they are related (Craver, 2007), while interventionist accounts require that causal claims be testable in a counterfactual sense (Woodward, 2005).
text.formatted: Mechanistic approaches call for the explicit identification of the components and the way in which they are related <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Craver, 2007)</ref>, while interventionist accounts require that causal claims be testable in a counterfactual sense <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Woodward, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: When these standards are applied to research into consciousness, they demand the introduction of bridge principles that connect neural observables to experiential constructs and prediction tables which list both the results that confirm and those that disconfirm the theories (Feest, 2022a; 2022b; Koch et al., 2016).
text.formatted: When these standards are applied to research into consciousness, they demand the introduction of bridge principles that connect neural observables to experiential constructs and prediction tables which list both the results that confirm and those that disconfirm the theories <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Feest, 2022a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">2022b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Koch et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The latest suggestions for methodological reform show this shift towards disciplined induction.

Michel and Morales (2020) propose a criterion of theoretical discriminability, which means that competing theories must produce incompatible and testable predictions, not merely gather empirical evidence.

The present framework goes further than these reformist ideas by incorporating three methodological elements: operational vocabularies (in order to make the theoretical constructs such as access, arousal, and valuation clearer), bridge principles (to define the mappings from observables to supposed experiences), and prediction tables (to spot falsifiers and counterfactuals).
In this way, criticism is turned into method.

In both philosophy and neuroscience, a single methodological requirement arises: induction should be kept as being empirically bounded, conceptually transparent, and causally testable (Feest, 2022a; 2022b; Koch et al., 2016).

Syntheses based on empirical evidence that are intended to find the minimal sufficient conditions for consciousness (Coppola, 2025) are useful for integrating different views but show the main epistemic risk that this paper has identified: the gradual shift of inductive plausibility into categorical sufficiency.
text.formatted: Syntheses based on empirical evidence that are intended to find the minimal sufficient conditions for consciousness <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Coppola, 2025)</ref> are useful for integrating different views but show the main epistemic risk that this paper has identified: the gradual shift of inductive plausibility into categorical sufficiency.

text.text: This epistemic dilemma also applies to the theoretical frameworks that form much of current consciousness research.

Global Neuronal Workspace theory (Mashour et al., 2020) and predictive-processing frameworks (Hohwy & Seth, 2020) each convert inductive regularities into formal causal schemes-the first by means of the idea of cortical ignition and the second through hierarchical prediction error minimization.
text.formatted: Global Neuronal Workspace theory (Mashour et al., 2020) and predictive-processing frameworks (Hohwy & Seth, 2020) each convert inductive regularities into formal causal schemes-the first by means of the idea of cortical ignition and the second through hierarchical prediction error minimization.

text.text: Although both have contributed to empirical unification, they both run the risk of treating inductive coherence as if it were ontological sufficiency.

A deflationary inductivism regards these models not as opposing metaphysical programmes but as disciplined tools within an evidential economy: their claims stay local, their bridge principles are made explicit, and their potential falsifiers are listed.
Within this limited framework, integration becomes a methodological rather than a metaphysical issue, allowing for pluralism without leading to overreach.
Induction's strength is in its scope, but its danger is in taking that scope to mean necessity.
Consciousness science, more than any other field, relies on inference while at the same time risking overreach (Seth & Bayne, 2022).
text.formatted: Consciousness science, more than any other field, relies on inference while at the same time risking overreach <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Seth & Bayne, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: A pragmatic philosophy of science must therefore recognize the indispensable role of induction while at the same time restraining its tendency to overextend (Feest, 2022a; 2022b; Brigandt, 2010).
text.formatted: A pragmatic philosophy of science must therefore recognize the indispensable role of induction while at the same time restraining its tendency to overextend <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Feest, 2022a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">2022b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Brigandt, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: As Martínez (2025) points out, cognitive representation itself involves a balance between informational rate, distortion, and complexity; a balance that is also present in inductive reasoning.

The empirical richness must be balanced against evidential distortion and conceptual excess: over-compression (drawing universal conclusions from limited data) simplifies at the expense of truth, while over-complexity diminishes explanatory clarity.
The task, then, is not to go beyond induction, but to bring discipline to its economy.

This deflationary inductivism is in line with pluralist and pragmatic philosophies of science which prefer local, model-relative generalizations to universal unification (Feest, 2022a; 2022b; Brigandt, 2010; Colombo & Wright, 2017).
text.formatted: This deflationary inductivism is in line with pluralist and pragmatic philosophies of science which prefer local, model-relative generalizations to universal unification <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Feest, 2022a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">2022b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Brigandt, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Colombo & Wright, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: On this view, progress in consciousness science does not come from discovering a final, sufficient substrate, but from constructing bounded bridges between evidence and experience-bridges that remain transparent, open to revision, and ethically reflective (Koch et al., 2016; Feest, 2022a; 2022b).
text.formatted: On this view, progress in consciousness science does not come from discovering a final, sufficient substrate, but from constructing bounded bridges between evidence and experience-bridges that remain transparent, open to revision, and ethically reflective <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Koch et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Feest, 2022a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">2022b)</ref>.

text.text: The framework set out here, consisting of operational vocabularies, bridge principles, and prediction tables, offers a method for keeping induction testable, modular, and morally accountable (Feest, 2022a; 2022b; Penny et al., 2010).

text.text: It turns criticism into practice by making inductive commitments clear, the inferential boundaries obvious, and the predictions falsifiable (Woodward, 2005; Feest, 2022a; 2022b).
text.formatted: It turns criticism into practice by making inductive commitments clear, the inferential boundaries obvious, and the predictions falsifiable <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Woodward, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Feest, 2022a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">2022b)</ref>.

text.text: Consciousness science cannot avoid using induction; it can only decide how consciously it practices it.

A modest, transparent, and testable inductivism-one that places local adequacy above metaphysical aspirations-offers the most responsible way forward in a field where epistemic error and ethical consequences are inseparable (Feest, 2022a; 2022b; Yuste et al., 2017).

text.text: Although the framework presented here makes clear the epistemic structure of induction in the study of consciousness, it does not address its formal integration with computational and mechanistic models.

Future research should turn the prediction tables into explicit priors in the context of Bayesian model comparison, thus turning conceptual transparency into quantitative accountability (Etz & Vandekerckhove, 2018; Penny et al., 2010).

text.text: In the case of cognitive architectures and neural simulations, bridge principles could be implemented as representational constraints that serve to guide both the construction and the interpretation of the models (Martínez, 2025; Craver, 2007).

text.text: Further theoretical work is required in order to clarify how inductive and abductive reasoning interact during the process of theory formation.

Even though this paper has stressed the logic of generalization, hypothesis generation (abduction) and deductive testing still remain essential components of the inferential cycle (Peirce, 1992a; 1992b; Woodward, 2005).
text.formatted: Even though this paper has stressed the logic of generalization, hypothesis generation (abduction) and deductive testing still remain essential components of the inferential cycle <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Peirce, 1992a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">1992b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Woodward, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: If we can map out this interaction, it might show new ways of formalizing how theories of consciousness develop from initial exploratory conjectures to empirically limited generalisations (Feest, 2022a; 2022b).
text.formatted: If we can map out this interaction, it might show new ways of formalizing how theories of consciousness develop from initial exploratory conjectures to empirically limited generalisations <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Feest, 2022a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">2022b)</ref>.

text.text: Consciousness science cannot escape the need for induction, but it can discipline it.

The proposal put forward is practical rather than revolutionary in that it seeks to keep induction modest, open and capable of being tested by:  precisely defining theoretical constructs (e.g., access, arousal, valuation, metacognition, self-model);  making bridge principles explicit, linking observables to experiential claims; and  Producing prediction tables which record both cases that confirm and those that falsify the predictions, in connection with counterfactual interventions such as lesion, stimulation, or pharmacological manipulation (Koch et al., 2016; Penny et al., 2010; Woodward, 2005).

text.text: When it comes to the study of consciousness, humility does not mean retreating from knowledge but rather consists in methodological precision-that is, the discipline which makes genuine understanding possible.
This article presents a conceptual analysis and methodological framework.
It reports no original empirical dataset or computational analysis; the sources informing the analysis are cited in the text and reference list.
